analysis.one_liner: Strips tax breaks from corporations that lock out their workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Tester with no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When an employer locks out its workforce — withholding work to force employees into concessions — this bill would raise that corporation's income tax rate from 21% to 35%. It would also deny the company tax deductions and tax credits for wages paid to temporary replacement workers hired to do the locked-out employees' jobs. The bill never advanced beyond its introduction and committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers facing a lockout, who would keep more leverage in labor disputes because their employer could no longer use taxpayer-subsidized tax breaks to cushion the cost of the lockout.

how_it_helps.text: A corporation taking part in a labor lockout would pay the pre-2017 corporate rate of 35% instead of 21% for that year, raising the cost of using a lockout to extract concessions from employees [S2][S3].

The company could no longer deduct wages or benefits paid to temporary replacement workers, nor claim the research credit or work opportunity credit for those wages, so the lockout strategy would cost the employer more out of pocket [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that use lockouts against their employees would pay hundreds of millions more in taxes per lockout year and lose deductions on strikebreaker wages; the tax-writing process would also take on added complexity in defining 'labor lockout.'

drawbacks.text: Defining a 'labor lockout' requires line-drawing between offensive lockouts and defensive ones (for example, locking out employees ahead of a threatened strike), and misclassification could raise a company's tax rate unfairly [S2][S3].

The higher rate applies to the corporation's entire income for the year, not just income tied to the dispute, so a company with a profitable year unrelated to the lockout would pay far more than the lockout itself cost it [S3].

Critics of raising the corporate rate generally argue higher corporate taxes can be passed to workers and consumers over time; here that objection is limited because the penalty applies only to lockout participants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a narrow but genuinely coercive practice. Its main weakness is design, not purpose: taxing the whole year's income at 35% is a blunt instrument that could hit more than the lockout itself, and the lockout definition would invite disputes. Had it advanced, a narrower penalty would have served the same goal with less collateral cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no action on it before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Tester introduced the bill on May 20, 2019, and no senator cosponsored it [S1][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the record through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use lockouts kept the current tax treatment of that practice untouched, and the tax code continued to subsidize it. Workers gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and saw it referred to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chair Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party breakdown exists; it had a Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and died in committee, which was controlled by Republicans [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Corporations that use lockouts (heavy manufacturing, mining, utilities)
industries.note: These employers would lose a taxpayer subsidy for withholding work to force concessions, paying a 35% corporate rate and losing deductions on replacement-worker wages. Lockouts are rare but are used to break employee bargaining power, so the change would shift leverage toward workers. [S2][S3]

Lockout employers could no longer deduct wages paid for temporary replacement workers, reducing the incentive to hire temps to run operations during a lockout. Demand for strikebreaker staffing would fall. [S2][S3]
